Exact solitary wave solutions
for a coupled gKdV-Schrodinger system
by a new ODE reduction method

Stephen C. Anco1, James Hornick2,
Sicheng Zhao3, Thomas Wolf1

1Department of Mathematics and Statistics
Brock University
St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada

2Department of Mathematics and Statistics
McMaster University
Hamilton, Ontario, Canada

3Department of Mathematics and Statistics
Queen’s University
Kingston, Ontario, Canada
Abstract.

A new method is developed for finding exact solitary wave solutions of a generalized Korteweg-de Vries equation with pp-power nonlinearity coupled to a linear Schrödinger equation arising in many different physical applications. This method yields 22 solution families, with p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4. No solutions for p>1p>1 were known previously in the literature. For p=1p=1, four of the solution families contain bright/dark Davydov solitons of the 1st and 2nd kind, obtained in recent literature by basic ansatze applied to the ODE system for travelling waves. All of the new solution families have interesting features, including bright/dark peaks with (up to) pp symmetric pairs of side peaks in the amplitude and a kink profile for the nonlinear part in the phase. The present method is fully systematic and involves several novel steps which reduce the travelling wave ODE system to a single nonlinear base ODE for which all polynomial solutions are found by symbolic computation. It is applicable more generally to other coupled nonlinear dispersive wave equations as well as to nonlinear ODE systems of generalized Hénon-Heiles form.

1. Introduction

A wide class of physical wave propagation phenomena are modeled by nonlinear dispersive systems. The simplest model that combines dispersion and weak nonlinearity is given by the Korteweg-de Vries (KdV) equation ut+α​u​ux+β​ux​x​x=0u_{t}+\alpha uu_{x}+\beta u_{xxx}=0 for uni-directional wave motion u⁡(t,x)u(t,x), which describes [1, 2] surface waves in shallow water, internal waves in stratified fluids, ion-acoustic waves in plasmas, atmospheric Rossby waves, compression waves in granular chains, deformations of long-chain molecules and anharmonic lattices, and numerous other physical applications. Higher-order nonlinearities are of physical interest in several of these applications [3, 4, 5, 6].

In more complex physical systems, nonlinear dispersive wave motion is coupled to high-frequency waves, as modeled by a linear Schrödinger equation (LS) i​ψt+κ​ψx​x=σ​u​ψi\psi_{t}+\kappa\psi_{xx}=\sigma u\psi for ψ⁡(t,x)\psi(t,x) in which u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) acts as a potential well. Physical applications include electron propagation coupled to nonlinear ion-acoustic waves in a collisionless plasma [7, 8], resonant interaction of capillary-gravity waves and internal water waves [9], electron propagation along deformable molecular chains [10, 11, 12], and energy transport by electrons in anharmonic lattices [13, 14]. See Ref.[15, 16] for further discussion.

This motivates the study of a general coupled gKdV-LS system

ut+α​up​ux+β​ux​x​x\displaystyle u_{t}+\alpha u^{p}u_{x}+\beta u_{xxx} =γ​(|ψ|2)x,\displaystyle=\gamma(|\psi|^{2})_{x}, (1.1)
i​ψt+κ​ψx​x\displaystyle i\psi_{t}+\kappa\psi_{xx} =σ​u​ψ,\displaystyle=\sigma u\psi, (1.2)

where p>0p>0 is the nonlinearity power and α\alpha is the nonlinearity coefficient, β\beta and κ\kappa are the dispersion coefficients, while γ\gamma and σ\sigma are the coupling constants. All of these parameters are non-zero, real constants. Here, u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) is the (real) gKdV field and ψ\psi is the (complex) LS field, which respectively describe the wave amplitude or lattice deformation, and the electron wave function or envelope of high-frequency waves.

One main question is understanding the nature of coherent propagating structures in this system, in particular, solitary wave solutions of different shapes and subsonic/supersonic speeds. Such solutions have the form of phase-modulated travelling waves

u=U⁡(ξ),ψ=e−i​ω​t​Ψ​(ξ),ξ=x−c​t,u=U(\xi),\quad\psi=e^{-i\omega t}\Psi(\xi),\quad\xi=x-ct, (1.3)

where cc is the wave speed, and ω\omega is the frequency. In physical applications, a travelling wave is supersonic if c>0c>0 and subsonic if c<0c<0 [11, 13, 16]. Here UU is a real function and Ψ\Psi is a complex function, which satisfy a coupled nonlinear system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs)

β​U′′′+(α​Up−c)​U′+γ​(|Ψ|2)′=0,κ​Ψ′′−i​c​Ψ′+(σ​U+ω)​Ψ=0.\beta U^{\prime\prime\prime}+(\alpha U^{p}-c)U^{\prime}+\gamma(|\Psi|^{2})^{\prime}=0,\quad\kappa\Psi^{\prime\prime}-ic\Psi^{\prime}+(\sigma U+\omega)\Psi=0. (1.4)

Solitary wave solutions require that UU decays exponentially for large |ξ||\xi| to a constant, bb, and likewise that |Ψ||\Psi| has a similar decay.

For a KdV nonlinearity, p=1p=1, some exact solutions are known which were obtained by use of elementary ODE methods combined with trial ansatze [7, 13] and also by the bi-linear ansatz method [17]; for a mKdV nonlinearity, p=2p=2, only approximate solutions have been found [14]. No work has been done to-date on higher nonlinearities.

The primary goal of the present paper is to develop and apply a new general method that yields numerous exact families of solitary wave solutions (1.3). In total, nine solution families are obtained for p=1p=1, eight families for p=2p=2, four families for p=3p=3, and a single family for p=4p=4. All of the solutions are non-singular. The gKdV component U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) has

  • •

    sech-squared profile

  • •

    bright/dark peak with exponential decay

  • •

    width ww and height/depth hh related by w2​h∝|α|1p​|β|1p−2​|κ|3−2p/|σ|w^{2}h\propto|\alpha|^{\frac{1}{p}}|\beta|^{\frac{1}{p}-2}|\kappa|^{3-\frac{2}{p}}/|\sigma|

  • •

    zero or non-zero (asymptotic) background, bb

More interestingly, the magnitude of the LS component |Ψ⁡(ξ)||\Psi(\xi)| has

  • •

    bright/dark central peak

  • •

    asymptotic tail which is bright/dark relative to the central peak

  • •

    in some cases, symmetric pairs of side peaks (up to pp in total)

while the LS phase arg⁡(Ψ⁡(ξ))\arg(\Psi(\xi)) has

  • •

    a linear part c2​ξ\frac{c}{2}\xi

  • •

    in some cases, a nonlinear part with a kink profile

For p=2,3,4p=2,3,4, the solutions are new. For p=1p=1, five families are new, while the other four families contain the previously known solutions in Ref.[7, 13] as particular subfamilies. Qualitatively novel features are the kink part in the LS phase and the presence of multiple symmetric side peaks in the LS amplitude.

The new method consists of the following main steps:
(1) express the form of the travelling waves as a symmetry-invariant solution and obtain first integrals for the ODE system by use of multi-reduction symmetry theory [18];
(2) change to polar variables and apply a hodograph transformation that leads to a triangular (decoupled) system in which the base ODE has a polynomial form;
(3) employ a power-balance technique to determine the general form for polynomial solutions of the base ODE;
(4) characterize conditions under which such solutions yield solitary waves;
(5) with those conditions, solve an overdetermined algebraic system for the coefficients in the polynomial solutions along with the power pp and the parameters α,β,γ,κ,σ\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\kappa,\sigma in the original gKdV-LS system in addition to c,ω,bc,\omega,b in the form of the travelling wave.

This algebraic system is nonlinear, with pp appearing in exponents, and so it is very non-trivial to solve. All solutions are found by employing the symbolic computer algebra package Crack [24] which is able to do non-polynomial case distinctions and splittings systematically. There is a further non-trivial aspect, stemming from the conditions for a solution to yield a solitary wave. Some of these conditions consist of inequalities on the parameters in the solution, while each solution has a different subset of the parameters that are free, up to reparameterization freedom. An optimal choice of free parameters must be found so that all of the inequalities can be solved explicitly, thereby yielding the allowed kinematic region in parameter space. This is carried out by use of Maple, which is also used to verify the final simplified explicit form for each family of solitary wave solutions.

Some additional results are obtained. All Lie point symmetries and low-order conservation laws are derived for the coupled gKdV-LS system (1.1)–(1.2). Through these conservation laws, a variational principle for phase-modulated travelling waves (1.3) is found and conserved quantities describing mass, charge, energy, and momentum are evaluated for each family of solitary waves. The variational principle provides a starting point for analysis of stability of the solitary waves.

The present method is applicable more generally to other coupled nonlinear dispersive wave equations as well as to nonlinear ODE systems of generalized Hénon-Heiles form.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses the Hamiltonian and Lagrangian formulation of the coupled gKdV-LS system (1.1)–(1.2), and gives the dimensionless form of this system which is used for subsequent results. Section 3 gives the derivation of the Lie point symmetries and low-order conservation laws and describes the physical meaning of the conserved quantities. Section 4 states the variational principle for phase-modulated travelling waves and sets up the first two steps in the new method for finding solitary wave solutions. The remaining three steps in this method are carried out in section 5, and a classification of all of the solution families is provided. Section 6 outlines the main features of each family, including a few remarks on stability for these solitary wave solutions. Finally, some concluding remarks are made in section 7.

Computational steps of the method are given in Appendix A; the output for each case p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4 is shown in Appendix B, which also contains the solved inequalities giving the allowed kinematic region in parameter space for each solution family.

2. Hamiltonian structure and dimensionless form

The gKdV-LS system (1.1)–(1.2) has a Hamiltonian structure

∂∂t​(uψ)=𝒟​(δ​H/δ​uδ​H/δ​ψ¯)\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ \psi\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal{D}\begin{pmatrix}\delta H/\delta u\\ \delta H/\delta\bar{\psi}\end{pmatrix} (2.1)

in which

𝒟=diag⁡(Dx,−σγ​i)\mathcal{D}={\rm diag}(D_{x},-\tfrac{\sigma}{\gamma}i) (2.2)

is a Hamiltonian operator, and

H=∫ℝ(12​β​ux2−1(p+1)​(p+2)​α​up+2+(κ​γ/σ)​|ψx|2+γ​u​|ψ|2)​𝑑xH=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}\beta u_{x}^{2}-\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}\alpha u^{p+2}+(\kappa\gamma/\sigma)|\psi_{x}|^{2}+\gamma u|\psi|^{2}\big)\,dx (2.3)

is the Hamiltonian functional. The associated Poisson bracket is given by

{F,G}=Re​∫ℝ(δ​F/δ​uδ​F/δ​ψ¯)†​𝒟​(δ​G/δ​uδ​G/δ​ψ¯)​𝑑x,\{F,G\}={\rm Re}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\begin{pmatrix}\delta F/\delta u\\ \delta F/\delta\bar{\psi}\end{pmatrix}^{\dagger}\mathcal{D}\begin{pmatrix}\delta G/\delta u\\ \delta G/\delta\bar{\psi}\end{pmatrix}\,dx, (2.4)

where FF and GG are arbitrary functionals of uu, ψ\psi, ψ¯\bar{\psi} and their xx-derivatives. This bracket is skew and satisfies the Jacobi identity as a consequence of 𝒟\mathcal{D} being a Hamiltonian operator, as follows from general results in the theory of Hamiltonian PDEs [20].

A Lagrangian formulation can be obtained via introduction of a potential by u=θxu=\theta_{x}. The system (1.1)–(1.2) then takes the form

θt​x+α​θxp​θx​x+β​θx​x​x​x\displaystyle\theta_{tx}+\alpha\theta_{x}^{p}\theta_{xx}+\beta\theta_{xxxx} =γ​(|ψ|2)x,\displaystyle=\gamma(|\psi|^{2})_{x}, (2.5)
i​ψt+κ​ψx​x\displaystyle i\psi_{t}+\kappa\psi_{xx} =σ​θx​ψ,\displaystyle=\sigma\theta_{x}\psi, (2.6)

which is readily seen to be the Euler-Lagrange equations of the Lagrangian

L=−12​θt​θx−1(p+1)​(p+2)​θxp+2+12​β​θx​x2+12​(γ/σ)​i​(ψ¯t​ψ−ψ¯​ψt)+(γ​κ/σ)​|ψx|2+γ​θx​|ψ|2.L=-\tfrac{1}{2}\theta_{t}\theta_{x}-\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}\theta_{x}^{p+2}+\tfrac{1}{2}\beta\theta_{xx}^{2}+\tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma/\sigma)i(\bar{\psi}_{t}\psi-\bar{\psi}\psi_{t})+(\gamma\kappa/\sigma)|\psi_{x}|^{2}+\gamma\theta_{x}|\psi|^{2}. (2.7)

Specifically, δ​L/δ​θ=θt​x+α​θxp​θx​x+β​θx​x​x​x−γ​(|ψ|2)x\delta L/\delta\theta=\theta_{tx}+\alpha\theta_{x}^{p}\theta_{xx}+\beta\theta_{xxxx}-\gamma(|\psi|^{2})_{x} and i⁡(σ/γ)​δ​L/δ​ψ¯=i​ψt+κ​ψx​x−σ​θx​ψi(\sigma/\gamma)\delta L/\delta\bar{\psi}=i\psi_{t}+\kappa\psi_{xx}-\sigma\theta_{x}\psi.

2.1. Dimensionless variables

It will be convenient to work in dimensionless variables, whereby the number of constants in the system (1.1)–(1.2) is reduced from five to one.

Proposition 1.

The dimensionless form of the gKdV-LS system (1.1)–(1.2) is given by

ut+s1​up​ux+ux​x​x+s2​(|ψ|2)x=0,\displaystyle u_{t}+s_{1}u^{p}u_{x}+u_{xxx}+s_{2}(|\psi|^{2})_{x}=0, (2.8)
i​ψt+ψx​x+k​u​ψ=0,\displaystyle i\psi_{t}+\psi_{xx}+ku\psi=0, (2.9)

where

s1={1,p= odd sgn⁡(α)​sgn​(β),p= even ,s2={−sgn⁡(α)​sgn​(γ),p= odd 1,p= even s_{1}=\begin{cases}1,&p=\text{ odd }\\ {\rm sgn}(\alpha){\rm sgn}(\beta),&p=\text{ even }\end{cases},\quad s_{2}=\begin{cases}-{\rm sgn}(\alpha){\rm sgn}(\gamma),&p=\text{ odd }\\ 1,&p=\text{ even }\end{cases} (2.10)

and

k=s2sgn(β)sgn(γ)sgn(κ)σ|β|2−1/p|α|−1/p/|κ|3−2/p.k=s_{2}\;{\rm sgn}(\beta){\rm sgn}(\gamma){\rm sgn}(\kappa)\sigma|\beta|^{2-1/p}|\alpha|^{-1/p}/|\kappa|^{3-2/p}. (2.11)

The transformation to this form is given by

λ1=β/κ,λ2=β2/κ3,|λ3|=(κ2/|αβ|)1/p,λ4=(κ2/|β|)1+1/p/(|α|1/p​|γ|),sgn⁡(λ3)={sgn⁡(α)​sgn​(β),p​ is odd−sgn⁡(β)​sgn​(γ),p​ is even.\begin{gathered}\lambda_{1}=\beta/\kappa,\quad\lambda_{2}=\beta^{2}/\kappa^{3},\quad|\lambda_{3}|=(\kappa^{2}/|\alpha\beta|)^{1/p},\quad\lambda_{4}=\sqrt{(\kappa^{2}/|\beta|)^{1+1/p}/(|\alpha|^{1/p}|\gamma|)},\\ {\rm sgn}(\lambda_{3})=\begin{cases}{\rm sgn}(\alpha){\rm sgn}(\beta),&p\text{ is odd}\\ -{\rm sgn}(\beta){\rm sgn}(\gamma),&p\text{ is even}\end{cases}.\end{gathered} (2.12)

Note that the sign s1s_{1} of the nonlinear convective term in equation (2.8) has been chosen to match the conventional form of the gKdV equation. The signs s1s_{1} and s2s_{2}, along with sgn⁡(k){\rm sgn}(k), control the sign properties of the Hamiltonian, as discussed in subsection 3.1.

α→λ1−1λ2λ3pα=α~,β→λ1−3λ2β=β~,γ→λ1−1λ2λ3−1λ42γ=γ~,κ→λ1−2λ2κ=κ~,σ→λ2λ3σ=σ~.\begin{gathered}\alpha\to\lambda_{1}^{-1}\lambda_{2}^{\mathstrut}\lambda_{3}^{p}\alpha=\tilde{\alpha},\quad\beta\to\lambda_{1}^{-3}\lambda_{2}^{\mathstrut}\beta=\tilde{\beta},\\ \gamma\to\lambda_{1}^{-1}\lambda_{2}^{\mathstrut}\lambda_{3}^{-1}\lambda_{4}^{2}\gamma=\tilde{\gamma},\quad\kappa\to\lambda_{1}^{-2}\lambda_{2}^{\mathstrut}\kappa=\tilde{\kappa},\quad\sigma\to\lambda_{2}\lambda_{3}\sigma=\tilde{\sigma}.\end{gathered} (2.14)

3. Symmetries and conservation laws

The symmetry group of the scaled gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) will provide a foundation for the subsequent analysis. Generators of continuous point symmetries can be obtained by the standard Lie symmetry method [20, 21], which yields the following result.

Proposition 2.

(i) The continuous symmetries of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) for general p≠0p\neq 0 are generated by

𝐗1=∂t,𝐗2=∂x,𝐗3=iψ∂ψ−iψ¯∂ψ¯.\mathbf{X}_{1}=\partial_{t},\quad\mathbf{X}_{2}=\partial_{x},\quad\mathbf{X}_{3}=i\psi\partial_{\psi}-i\bar{\psi}\partial_{\bar{\psi}}. (3.1)

Respectively, they comprise time-translations, space-translations, and phase rotations,

t→t+ϵ1,x→x+ϵ2,ψ→exp⁡(i​ϵ3)​ψ,t\to t+\epsilon_{1},\quad x\to x+\epsilon_{2},\quad\psi\to\exp(i\epsilon_{3})\psi, (3.2)

where ϵ1\epsilon_{1}, ϵ2\epsilon_{2}, ϵ3\epsilon_{3} ∈ℝ\in{\mathbb{R}} are group parameters. (ii) Additional continuous symmetries arise only for p=1p=1. They are generated by

𝐗4=t∂x+∂u+(s1kt+12x)(iψ∂ψ−iψ¯∂ψ¯),\mathbf{X}_{4}=t\partial_{x}+\partial_{u}+(s_{1}kt+\tfrac{1}{2}x)(i\psi\partial_{\psi}-i\bar{\psi}\partial_{\bar{\psi}}), (3.3)

which constitutes a Galilean boost

x→x+ϵ4​t,u→u+ϵ4,ψ→exp⁡(i⁡(ϵ4​(k​t+12​x)+ϵ4​142​t))​ψ\quad x\to x+\epsilon_{4}t,\quad u\to u+\epsilon_{4},\quad\psi\to\exp\big(i(\epsilon_{4}(kt+\tfrac{1}{2}x)+\epsilon_{4}{}^{2}\tfrac{1}{4}t)\big)\psi (3.4)

with group parameter ϵ4\epsilon_{4} ∈ℝ\in{\mathbb{R}}.

These transformations (3.2) and (3.4) generate, respectively, a three-dimensional abelian symmetry group and a four-dimensional non-abelian symmetry group with the commutator structure

[𝐗1,𝐗4]=𝐗2+s1​k​𝐗3,[𝐗2,𝐗4]=𝐗3.[\mathbf{X}_{1},\mathbf{X}_{4}]=\mathbf{X}_{2}+s_{1}k\mathbf{X}_{3},\quad[\mathbf{X}_{2},\mathbf{X}_{4}]=\mathbf{X}_{3}. (3.5)

The gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) also possesses a discrete point symmetry t→−tt\to-t, x→−xx\to-x, ψ→ψ¯\psi\to\bar{\psi}, which is a space-time reflection combined with complex conjugation.

3.1. Conservation laws

A conservation law is a continuity equation

Dt​T+Dx​X=0D_{t}T+D_{x}X=0 (3.6)

that holds for all formal solutions (u⁡(t,x),ψ⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),\psi(t,x)) of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9), where DtD_{t} and DxD_{x} denote total derivatives with respect to tt and xx, which act by the chain rule [20, 21]. Here TT is the conserved density and XX is the spatial flux; the pair (T,X)(T,X) is called the conserved current. In general, TT and XX can be functions of tt, xx, uu, ψ\psi, ψ¯\bar{\psi}, and xx-derivatives of uu, ψ\psi, ψ¯\bar{\psi}, with tt-derivatives being eliminated through the equations (2.8) and (2.9).

Conservation laws in which T=Dx​ΘT=D_{x}\Theta and X=−Dt​ΘX=-D_{t}\Theta hold for all formal solutions (u⁡(t,x),ψ⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),\psi(t,x)) are trivial, since the continuity equation reduces to an identity via commutativity of derivatives. Trivial conservation laws thus contain no information about solutions. Any conservation laws that differ just by a trivial conservation law can be viewed as being locally equivalent. Consequently, only non-trivial conservation laws up to local equivalence are of interest.

Any non-trivial conservation law yields a corresponding conserved integral ∫ΩT​𝑑x\int_{\Omega}T\,dx which satisfies dd​t​∫ΩT​𝑑x=−X|∂Ω\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega}T\,dx=-X|_{\partial\Omega}, on any given spatial domain Ω⊂ℝ\Omega\subset{\mathbb{R}} of interest. Under appropriate boundary conditions posed at ∂Ω\partial\Omega for solutions (u⁡(t,x),ψ⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),\psi(t,x)), the conserved integral will be time-independent. In the situation when Ω=ℝ\Omega={\mathbb{R}} is the real line, the necessary boundary conditions take the form of spatial decay conditions on u⁡(t,x)u(t,x) and |ψ⁡(t,x)||\psi(t,x)| as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, so that the spatial flux X→0X\to 0, whereby

dd​t​∫ℝT​𝑑x=0.\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb{R}}T\,dx=0. (3.7)

Note that the conserved integral ∫ℝT​𝑑x\int_{\mathbb{R}}T\,dx is unchanged if TT is replaced by a locally equivalent conserved density, satisfying suitable spatial decay conditions. The differential order of a conserved integral will refer to the minimum of the differential orders of all conserved densities that are locally equivalent to TT. Conserved integrals of most physical interest typically have a differential order that is no higher than the differential order of the Hamiltonian.

For the method applied in subsequent sections for deriving explicit solutions (u⁡(t,x),ψ⁡(t,x))(u(t,x),\psi(t,x)) of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9), it will be essential to know both the conserved density TT and the spatial flux XX in a conservation law.

The generators of continuous point symmetries can be used to obtain conservation laws of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) through the Hamiltonian version of Noether’s theorem. Additional conservation laws arise from the Casimirs of the Hamiltonian structure.

Alternatively, conservation laws can be obtained directly by use of the standard multiplier method [20, 21, 22, 23, 24], which does not rely on existence of any variational structure.

Both of these methods for finding conservation laws yield the following result.

Proposition 3.

For general p≠0p\neq 0, all non-trivial conservation laws of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) with conserved densities of differential order at most 11 are spanned by the conserved currents

T1=u,X1=ux​x+s11p+1up+1+s2|ψ|2;\displaystyle\begin{aligned} T_{1}=u,\quad X_{1}=u_{xx}+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{p+1}u^{p+1}+s_{2}|\psi|^{2};\end{aligned} (3.8)
T2=12|ψ|2,X2=|ψ|2arg(ψ)x;\displaystyle\begin{aligned} T_{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}|\psi|^{2},\quad X_{2}=|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{x};\end{aligned} (3.9)
T3=12​k​u2−s2​|ψ|2​arg⁡(ψ)x,X3=k⁡(u​ux​x−12​ux2+s1​1p+2​up+2)−s2​|ψx|2+s2​|ψ|2​arg⁡(ψ)t;\displaystyle\begin{aligned} T_{3}&=\tfrac{1}{2}ku^{2}-s_{2}|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{x},\\ X_{3}&=k(uu_{xx}-\tfrac{1}{2}u_{x}^{2}+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{p+2}u^{p+2})-s_{2}|\psi_{x}|^{2}+s_{2}|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{t};\end{aligned} (3.10)

Additional conservation laws of differential order at most 11 arise only for p=1p=1. They are spanned by

T5\displaystyle T_{5} =s2​k​(12​t​u2−s1​x​u)−t​|ψ|2​arg⁡(ψ)x+(s1​k​t+12​x)​|ψ|2,\displaystyle=s_{2}k(\tfrac{1}{2}tu^{2}-s_{1}xu)-t|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{x}+(s_{1}kt+\tfrac{1}{2}x)|\psi|^{2}, (3.12)

+t​|ψ|2​arg⁡(ψ)t+(s1​2​k​t+x)​|ψ|2​arg⁡(ψ)x.\displaystyle+t|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{t}+(s_{1}2kt+x)|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{x}.

The corresponding conserved integrals consist of

M=∫ℝu​𝑑xmass,\displaystyle{M}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}u\,dx\quad\text{mass,} (3.13)
J=∫ℝ12​|ψ|2​𝑑xcharge,\displaystyle{J}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\tfrac{1}{2}|\psi|^{2}\,dx\quad\text{charge,} (3.14)
P=∫ℝ(12​u2−s2​1k​|ψ|2​arg⁡(ψ)x)​𝑑xmomentum,\displaystyle{P}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}u^{2}-s_{2}\tfrac{1}{k}|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{x}\big)\,dx\quad\text{momentum,} (3.15)
H=∫ℝ(12​ux2−s1​1(p+1)​(p+2)​up+2+s2​1k​|ψx|2−s2​u​|ψ|2)​𝑑x(Hamiltonian) energy,\displaystyle{H}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}u_{x}^{2}-s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}u^{p+2}+s_{2}\tfrac{1}{k}|\psi_{x}|^{2}-s_{2}u|\psi|^{2}\big)\,dx\quad\text{(Hamiltonian) energy,} (3.16)

for p≠0p\neq 0, and

G=∫ℝ(s2​k​(12​t​u2−s1​x​u)−t​|ψ|2​arg⁡(ψ)x+(s1​k​t+12​x)​|ψ|2)​𝑑xGalilean momentum\displaystyle{G}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\big(s_{2}k(\tfrac{1}{2}tu^{2}-s_{1}xu)-t|\psi|^{2}\arg(\psi)_{x}+(s_{1}kt+\tfrac{1}{2}x)|\psi|^{2}\big)\,dx\quad\text{Galilean momentum} (3.17)

for p=1p=1.

With respect to the Hamiltonian structure (2.1)–(2.2), mass is a Casimir, while charge, momentum, energy, and Galilean momentum arise respectively from the phase rotation symmetry, space-translation symmetry, time-translation symmetry. and Galilean boost symmetry. Two remarks on these conserved integrals will be worthwhile.

The energy (Hamiltonian) will be non-negative when s1=−1s_{1}=-1, s2=sgn⁡(k)=−sgn⁡(u)s_{2}={\rm sgn}(k)=-{\rm sgn}(u), and otherwise it will have an indefinite sign. The sign of s1s_{1} controls the gKdV portion of the energy, while the signs of s2s_{2} and kk control the LS portion. When the sign is indefinite, conservation of energy does not preclude blow-up of |u||u|, |ux||u_{x}|, |ψ||\psi|, |ψx||\psi_{x}| caused by concentration of the energy density, which is referred to as focusing; in contrast, when the sign is non-negative, conservation of energy prevents such blow-up, which is referred to as defocusing (see e.g. Ref.[25]).

The Galilean momentum can be expressed as G=k​t​(s2​P+s1​J)−χ⁡(t){G}=kt(s_{2}{P}+s_{1}{J})-\chi(t) where χ⁡(t)=∫ℝ(s1​s2​k​u−12​|ψ|2)​x​𝑑x\chi(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}(s_{1}s_{2}ku-\tfrac{1}{2}|\psi|^{2})x\,dx is like a center of mass-charge. In particular, under decay conditions such that G{G}, P{P}, J{J} are conserved integrals, χ⁡(t)\chi(t) satisfies dd​t​χ​(t)=k⁡(s2​P+s1​J)\frac{d}{dt}\chi(t)=k(s_{2}{P}+s_{1}{J}). This implies χ⁡(t)=χ⁡(0)+t​V\chi(t)=\chi(0)+tV, where V=k⁡(s2​P+s1​J)V=k(s_{2}{P}+s_{1}{J}) is the speed at which the center of mass-charge moves.

4. ODE system for phase-modulated travelling waves

Phase-modulated travelling waves (1.3) have a symmetry characterization that they are invariant under a Galilean transformation x→x+c​ϵx\to x+c\epsilon, t→t+ϵt\to t+\epsilon to a reference frame moving with speed cc, combined with a phase rotation ψ→e−i​ω​ϵ​ψ\psi\to e^{-i\omega\epsilon}\psi having angular speed ω\omega. Specifically, the symmetry generator

𝐗=∂t+c∂x−iωψ∂ψ+iωψ¯∂ψ¯\mathbf{X}=\partial_{t}+c\partial_{x}-i\omega\psi\partial_{\psi}+i\omega\bar{\psi}\partial_{\bar{\psi}} (4.1)

has the invariants U=uU=u, Ψ=ei​ω​t​ψ\Psi=e^{i\omega t}\psi, ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct, and hence a phase-modulated travelling wave is an invariant solution of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) under this symmetry.

Substitution of the invariant form (1.3) into the coupled equations (2.8) and (2.9) yields a coupled nonlinear ODE system for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) and Ψ⁡(ξ)\Psi(\xi):

U′′′+(s1​Up−c)​U′+s2​(|Ψ|2)′=0,\displaystyle U^{\prime\prime\prime}+(s_{1}U^{p}-c)U^{\prime}+s_{2}(|\Psi|^{2})^{\prime}=0, (4.2a)
Ψ′′−i​c​Ψ′+(k​U+ω)​Ψ=0.\displaystyle\Psi^{\prime\prime}-ic\Psi^{\prime}+(kU+\omega)\Psi=0. (4.2b)

It will be useful to consider the polar form of this system, which arises from expressing Ψ\Psi in amplitude-phase form

Ψ=A​exp⁡(i​Φ).\Psi=A\exp(i\Phi). (4.3)

The polar variables A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) and Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi), along with U⁡(ξ)U(\xi), satisfy the coupled nonlinear ODEs

U′′′+(s1​Up−c)​U′+2​s2​A​A′=0,\displaystyle U^{\prime\prime\prime}+(s_{1}U^{p}-c)U^{\prime}+2s_{2}AA^{\prime}=0, (4.4a)
A′′+(kU+cΦ′−Φ′+2ω)A=0,\displaystyle A^{\prime\prime}+(kU+c\Phi^{\prime}-\Phi^{\prime}{}^{2}+\omega)A=0, (4.4b)
A​Φ′′+(2​Φ′−c)​A′=0.\displaystyle A\Phi^{\prime\prime}+(2\Phi^{\prime}-c)A^{\prime}=0. (4.4c)

4.1. Variational formulation and symmetries

The ODE system (4.4) for phase-modulated travelling waves has a variational formulation in terms of the conserved integrals (3.13)–(3.16) for mass, charge, momentum, and energy evaluated for solutions U⁡(ξ)U(\xi), A⁡(ξ)A(\xi), Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi). These conserved integrals consist of

M⁡[U]=∫−∞∞U​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle{M}[U]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}U\,d\xi, (4.5)
J⁡[A]=∫−∞∞12​A2​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle{J}[A]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\tfrac{1}{2}A^{2}\,d\xi, (4.6)
P⁡[U,A,Φ]=∫−∞∞(12​U2−s2​1k​A2​Φ′)​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle{P}[U,A,\Phi]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\tfrac{1}{2}U^{2}-s_{2}\tfrac{1}{k}A^{2}\Phi^{\prime})\,d\xi, (4.7)
H[U,A,Φ]=∫−∞∞(12U′−2s11(p+1)​(p+2)Up+2+s21k(A′+2A2Φ′)2−s2UA2)dξ.\displaystyle{H}[U,A,\Phi]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\tfrac{1}{2}U^{\prime}{}^{2}-s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}U^{p+2}+s_{2}\tfrac{1}{k}(A^{\prime}{}^{2}+A^{2}\Phi^{\prime}{}^{2})-s_{2}UA^{2})\,d\xi. (4.8)

Consider the conserved integral

W⁡[U,A,Φ]=H⁡[U,A,Φ]+c​P​[U,A,Φ]−s2​(2​ω/k)​J​[A]+C1​M​[U],W[U,A,\Phi]={H}[U,A,\Phi]+c{P}[U,A,\Phi]-s_{2}(2\omega/k){J}[A]+C_{1}{M}[U], (4.9)

where C1C_{1} is an arbitrary constant. Then the three ODEs (4.4a), (4.4b), (4.4c) are respectively equivalent to the Euler-Lagrange equations

(δ​W/δ​Uδ​W/δ​Aδ​W/δ​Φ)=0.\begin{pmatrix}\delta W/\delta U\\ \delta W/\delta A\\ \delta W/\delta\Phi\end{pmatrix}=0. (4.10)

In particular, the first of these equations yields the integral of ODE (4.4a) with C1C_{1} being the constant of integration.

This variational formulation is a generalization of the known variational formulations respectively for travelling waves of the gKdV equation [26] and phase-modulated travelling waves of the Schrödinger equation [27].

The Euler-Lagrange equations (4.10) manifestly inherit a translation symmetry and a phase-shift symmetry

𝐗trans.=∂ξ,𝐗phas.=∂Φ\mathbf{X}_{\rm trans.}=\partial_{\xi},\quad\mathbf{X}_{\rm phas.}=\partial_{\Phi} (4.11)

from the symmetries of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9). A complete classification of all continuous symmetries is straightforwardly obtained by the Lie symmetry method.

Proposition 4.

(i) For general p≠0p\neq 0, the continuous symmetries of the Euler-Lagrange equations (4.10) are generated by the translation and phase-shift symmetries (4.11), which yield the transformation groups ξ→ξ+ϵ\xi\to\xi+\epsilon and Φ→Φ+ϵ\Phi\to\Phi+\epsilon, where ϵ∈ℝ\epsilon\in{\mathbb{R}} is the group parameter for each transformation. (ii) Additional symmetries exist only when p=1p=1. They are generated by

𝐗scal.=−ξ∂ξ+2(U−s1c)∂U+2A∂A−c2ξ∂Φ,\displaystyle\mathbf{X}_{\rm scal.}=-\xi\partial_{\xi}+2(U-s_{1}c)\partial_{U}+2A\partial_{A}-\frac{c}{2}\xi\partial_{\Phi}, (4.12)
ω=−s1kc−c24,C1=−s1c22,p=1,\displaystyle\omega=-s_{1}kc-\frac{c^{2}}{4},\quad C_{1}=-s_{1}\frac{c^{2}}{2},\quad p=1,

which yields the scaling-type transformation group ξ→λ−1​ξ\xi\to\lambda^{-1}\xi, U→λ2​U+s1​c​(1−λ2)U\to\lambda^{2}U+s_{1}c(1-\lambda^{2}), A→λ2​AA\to\lambda^{2}A, Φ→Φ+(1−λ−1)​c​ξ/2\Phi\to\Phi+(1-\lambda^{-1})c\xi/2, where λ≠0∈ℝ\lambda\neq 0\in{\mathbb{R}} is the group parameter.

These symmetries have a key role in the analysis of stability of solutions.

4.2. Reduction to a decoupled second-order ODE

Ideally, the goal would be to solve the ODE system (4.4) in explicit form for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi), A⁡(ξ)A(\xi), Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi). Note that physically non-trivial solutions must have U′≢0U^{\prime}\not\equiv 0 and A′≢0A^{\prime}\not\equiv 0.

This system consists of one third-order ODE (4.4a) and two second-order ODEs (4.4b) and (4.4c). Therefore, finding the general solution would require a total of seven integrations. As noted in the work Ref.[13, 14], inspection of the ODEs suggest that only a few explicit integrations are possible.

Nevertheless, remarkably, the system (4.4) can be reduced to a single second-order ODE from which U⁡(ξ)U(\xi), A⁡(ξ)A(\xi), Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi) can be obtained by quadratures. This reduction is found by the following new method which involves two main steps.

In the first step, symmetry multi-reduction is applied, which gives a set of three functionally independent first integrals. These first integrals arise from conservation laws of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) such that the conservation law is invariant (up to local equivalence) under the symmetry (4.1) which characterizes phase-modulated travelling waves. The multi-reduction method yields the first integrals directly, without the need to know in advance any conservation laws. From the first integrals, an explicit reduction to a system of one second-order ODE and two first-order ODEs is obtained.

The second step starts from observing that the resulting second-order ODE in the first step can be expressed in the form of a nonlinear oscillator equation. This equation admits an energy-type first integral, which can be combined with the remaining two first-order ODEs to get a decoupled second-order ODE by employing a hodograph transformation. The resulting system of ODEs is triangular such that every solution of the transformed second-order ODE yields a solution (U⁡(ξ)CLOSE(U(\xi), A⁡(ξ)A(\xi), OPENΦ⁡(ξ))\Phi(\xi)) by quadratures. Furthermore, two of these quadratures can be carried out explicitly to obtain U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) and A⁡(ξ)A(\xi), while Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi) is expressed as a final quadrature in terms of (U⁡(ξ),A⁡(ξ))(U(\xi),A(\xi)).

The preceding steps will be carried out in the next subsections.

4.3. First integrals from symmetry multi-reduction

The first step consists of deriving first integrals of the ODE system (4.4) by use of the method of symmetry multi-reduction [18]. This method relies on the property if a conservation law (3.6) of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) is invariant under the symmetry (4.1) that characterizes the ODE system, then the conserved density TT and the flux XX yield a first integral d​Cd​ξ=0\tfrac{dC}{d\xi}=0 given by

C=(X−c​T)|u=U,ψ=ei​ω​t​Ψ=const.C=(X-cT)|_{u=U,\psi=e^{i\omega t}\Psi}=\text{const.} (4.13)

for all solutions (U⁡(ξ)CLOSE(U(\xi), A⁡(ξ)A(\xi), OPENΦ⁡(ξ))\Phi(\xi)). This expression (4.13) has the physical meaning of the net flux in the moving reference frame of travelling wave.

All symmetry-invariant conservation laws can be derived in a systematic way based on the use of multipliers. Specifically, there is an explicit condition characterizing multipliers that yield symmetry-invariant conservation laws.

For the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9), a multiplier is a pair of functions (Qu,Qψ)(Q^{u},Q^{\psi}) of tt, xx, uu, ψ\psi, ψ¯\bar{\psi}, and xx-derivatives of uu, ψ\psi, ψ¯\bar{\psi}, such that

(ut+s1​up​ux+ux​x​x+s2​(|ψ|2)x)​Qu+(i​ψt+ψx​x+k​u​ψ)​Qψ+(−i​ψ¯t+ψ¯x​x+k​u​ψ¯)​Q¯ψ\displaystyle(u_{t}+s_{1}u^{p}u_{x}+u_{xxx}+s_{2}(|\psi|^{2})_{x})Q^{u}+(i\psi_{t}+\psi_{xx}+ku\psi)Q^{\psi}+(-i\bar{\psi}_{t}+\bar{\psi}_{xx}+ku\bar{\psi})\bar{Q}^{\psi} (4.14)
=Dt​T+Dx​X\displaystyle=D_{t}T+D_{x}X

for some functions TT and XX. Since the system (2.8)–(2.9) is comprised of evolution equations, the general theory of multipliers shows that, firstly, every non-trivial conservation law (up to local equivalence) will arise from a multiplier, and that, secondly, multipliers are related to (T,X)(T,X) by a variational derivative, Qu=Eu​(T)Q^{u}=E_{u}(T) and Qψ=Eψ¯​(T)Q^{\psi}=E_{\bar{\psi}}(T), where EvE_{v} denotes the Euler operator (variational derivative) with respect to a variable vv. These expressions show that any conserved density of differential order at most 11 will arise from a multiplier of differential order at most 22. Hence, only multipliers given by functions of tt, xx, uu, ψ\psi, ψ¯\bar{\psi}, and xx-derivatives of uu, ψ\psi, ψ¯\bar{\psi} up to second-order will be considered hereafter.

All multipliers of differential order at most 22 are the solutions of the linear system of determining equations

Ev​((ut+s1​up​ux+ux​x​x+s2​(|ψ|2)x)​Qu+(i​ψt+ψx​x+k​u)​Qψ+(−i​ψ¯t+ψ¯x​x+k​u​ψ¯)​Q¯ψ)\displaystyle E_{v}\big((u_{t}+s_{1}u^{p}u_{x}+u_{xxx}+s_{2}(|\psi|^{2})_{x})Q^{u}+(i\psi_{t}+\psi_{xx}+ku)Q^{\psi}+(-i\bar{\psi}_{t}+\bar{\psi}_{xx}+ku\bar{\psi})\bar{Q}^{\psi}\big) (4.15)
=0,v={u,ψ,ψ¯}.\displaystyle=0,\quad v=\{u,\psi,\bar{\psi}\}.

These three equations split with respect to utu_{t}, ψt\psi_{t}, ψ¯t\bar{\psi}_{t}, and their xx-derivatives, yielding an overdetermined linear system for (Qu,Qψ)(Q^{u},Q^{\psi}). For each solution, a corresponding conserved current (T,X)(T,X) can be recovered by use of a homotopy integral formula.

The theory of symmetry multi-reduction shows that the condition for a multiplier to yield a symmetry-invariant conservation law is given by pr​𝐗​(Qu,Qψ)=0{\rm pr}\mathbf{X}(Q^{u},Q^{\psi})=0, where pr​𝐗{\rm pr}\mathbf{X} is the prolongation of the symmetry generator (4.1). This condition is a linear system of two equations

i​ω​(ψx​x​Qψx​xu−ψ¯x​x​Qψ¯x​xu+ψx​Qψxu−ψ¯x​Qψ¯xu+ψ​Qψu−ψ¯​Qψ¯u)−c​Qxu−Qtu=0,\displaystyle i\omega\big(\psi_{xx}Q^{u}_{\psi_{xx}}-\bar{\psi}_{xx}Q^{u}_{\bar{\psi}_{xx}}+\psi_{x}Q^{u}_{\psi_{x}}-\bar{\psi}_{x}Q^{u}_{\bar{\psi}_{x}}+\psi Q^{u}_{\psi}-\bar{\psi}Q^{u}_{\bar{\psi}}\big)-cQ^{u}_{x}-Q^{u}_{t}=0, (4.16a)
i​ω​(ψx​x​Qψx​xψ−ψ¯x​x​Qψ¯x​xψ+ψx​Qψxψ−ψ¯x​Qψ¯xψ+ψ​Qψψ−ψ¯​Qψ¯ψ+Qψ)−c​Qxψ−Qtψ=0.\displaystyle i\omega\big(\psi_{xx}Q^{\psi}_{\psi_{xx}}-\bar{\psi}_{xx}Q^{\psi}_{\bar{\psi}_{xx}}+\psi_{x}Q^{\psi}_{\psi_{x}}-\bar{\psi}_{x}Q^{\psi}_{\bar{\psi}_{x}}+\psi Q^{\psi}_{\psi}-\bar{\psi}Q^{\psi}_{\bar{\psi}}+Q^{\psi}\big)-cQ^{\psi}_{x}-Q^{\psi}_{t}=0. (4.16b)

Hence, all symmetry-invariant conservation laws arise from the solutions of the overdetermined linear system given by splitting the five equations (4.15)–(4.16) with respect to utu_{t}, ψt\psi_{t}, ψ¯t\bar{\psi}_{t}, and their xx-derivatives. Each solution (Qu,Qψ)(Q^{u},Q^{\psi}) determines a symmetry-invariant conserved current (T,X)(T,X) which in turn yields a first integral (4.13) of the ODE system (4.4).

The result is that the four conservation laws (3.8), (3.9), (3.10), (3.11) from Proposition 3 are symmetry invariant, while the fifth conservation law (3.12) which holds only for p=1p=1 is not symmetry invariant. Hence, symmetry multi-reduction yields four first integrals. In polar variables, they are given by

C1=U′′+s2​A2−c​U+s1​1p+1​Up+1,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} C_{1}=U^{\prime\prime}+s_{2}A^{2}-cU+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{p+1}U^{p+1},\end{aligned} (4.17)
C2=A2​(Φ′−12​c),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} C_{2}=A^{2}(\Phi^{\prime}-\tfrac{1}{2}c),\end{aligned} (4.18)
C3=k(UU′′−12U′2−12cU2+s11p+2Up+2)−s2A′2−s2A2(Φ′2+ω),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} C_{3}&=k(UU^{\prime\prime}-\tfrac{1}{2}U^{\prime}{}^{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}cU^{2}+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{p+2}U^{p+2})-s_{2}A^{\prime}{}^{2}-s_{2}A^{2}(\Phi^{\prime}{}^{2}+\omega),\end{aligned} (4.19)
C4=12k(U′′+s11p+1Up+1+s2A2)2−kc(12U′2+s11(p+1)​(p+2)Up+2)−s2cA′2−s2A2(cΦ′2+2ωΦ′+kcU).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} C_{4}&=\tfrac{1}{2}k(U^{\prime\prime}+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{p+1}U^{p+1}+s_{2}A^{2})^{2}-kc(\tfrac{1}{2}U^{\prime}{}^{2}+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}U^{p+2})\\ &\qquad-s_{2}cA^{\prime}{}^{2}-s_{2}A^{2}(c\Phi^{\prime}{}^{2}+2\omega\Phi^{\prime}+kcU).\end{aligned} (4.20)

It is straightforward to see that these first integrals satisfy an algebraic relation

12kC12−s22ωC2+cC3−C4=0,\tfrac{1}{2}kC_{1}{}^{2}-s_{2}2\omega C_{2}+cC_{3}-C_{4}=0, (4.21)

and so only three of them are functionally independent. This leads to the following result.

Lemma 1.

The conservation laws (3.8), (3.9), (3.10), (3.11) of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) yield three functionally independent first integrals of the ODE system (4.4) for phase-modulated travelling waves (1.3). This gives a reduction of this system to one second-order ODE and two first-order ODEs

U′′=c​U−s1​1p+1​Up+1−s2​A2+C1,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} U^{\prime\prime}=cU-s_{1}\tfrac{1}{p+1}U^{p+1}-s_{2}A^{2}+C_{1},\end{aligned} (4.22)
12kU′2+s2A′2=k​C1​U+12​k​c​U2−s1​1(p+2)​(p+1)​k​Up+2−s2​k​U​A2−s2​(14​c2+ω)​A2−s2​C2​A−22−C~3,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \tfrac{1}{2}kU^{\prime}{}^{2}+s_{2}A^{\prime}{}^{2}&=kC_{1}U+\tfrac{1}{2}kcU^{2}-s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+2)(p+1)}kU^{p+2}-s_{2}kUA^{2}\\ &\qquad-s_{2}(\tfrac{1}{4}c^{2}+\omega)A^{2}-s_{2}C_{2}{}^{2}A^{-2}-\tilde{C}_{3},\end{aligned} (4.23)
Φ′=12​c+C2​A−2,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \Phi^{\prime}=\tfrac{1}{2}c+C_{2}A^{-2},\end{aligned} (4.24)

where C1C_{1}, C2C_{2}, C~3\tilde{C}_{3} (=C3+s2​c​C2=C_{3}+s_{2}cC_{2}) are free parameters.

This completes the first step in the analysis.

4.4. Hodograph transformation to triangular form

The second step consists of showing that the ODE system (4.22)–(4.24) can be decoupled into a triangular form, without any assumptions.

Consider a hodograph transformation

A=F⁡(U).A=F(U). (4.25)

Note that, since non-trivial solutions of the ODE system (4.4) must have A≠const.A\neq\text{const.}, this transformation thereby exists (at least) locally.

Substitution of relation (4.25) into the system yields

U′′=c​U−s1​1p+1​Up+1−s2​F​(U)2+C1,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} U^{\prime\prime}=cU-s_{1}\tfrac{1}{p+1}U^{p+1}-s_{2}F(U)^{2}+C_{1},\end{aligned} (4.26)
U′2=(kC1U+12kcU2−s11(p+2)​(p+1)kUp+2−s2((14c2+ω)+kU)F(U)2−C~3)F(U)2−s2C22F​(U)2​(12​k+s2​F′​(U)2),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} U^{\prime}{}^{2}&=\frac{(kC_{1}U+\tfrac{1}{2}kcU^{2}-s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+2)(p+1)}kU^{p+2}-s_{2}((\tfrac{1}{4}c^{2}+\omega)+kU)F(U)^{2}-\tilde{C}_{3})F(U)^{2}-s_{2}C_{2}{}^{2}}{F(U)^{2}(\tfrac{1}{2}k+s_{2}F^{\prime}(U)^{2})},\end{aligned} (4.27)

The second-order ODE (4.26) now has the form of a nonlinear oscillator equation. It possesses the first integral

C~4=12U′+2s2G(U)+s11(p+1)​(p+2)Up+2−12cU2−C1U,\tilde{C}_{4}=\tfrac{1}{2}U^{\prime}{}^{2}+s_{2}G(U)+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}U^{p+2}-\tfrac{1}{2}cU^{2}-C_{1}U, (4.29)

where C~4\tilde{C}_{4} is a constant, and where

This gives

Equating equations (4.31) and (4.27), and replacing

F​(U)2=G′​(U),F′​(U)=2​G′′​(U)/F⁡(U),F(U)^{2}=G^{\prime}(U),\quad F^{\prime}(U)=2G^{\prime\prime}(U)/F(U), (4.32)

yields

12​(s2​G​(U)+s1​1(p+1)​(p+2)​Up+2−12​c​U2−C1​U−C~4)​G′′​(U)2\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}(s_{2}G(U)+s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}U^{p+2}-\tfrac{1}{2}cU^{2}-C_{1}U-\tilde{C}_{4})G^{\prime\prime}(U)^{2} (4.33)
=(kU+14c2+ω)G′(U)2−(kG(U)−s2(C~3+kC~4))G′(U)+C22,\displaystyle=(kU+\tfrac{1}{4}c^{2}+\omega)G^{\prime}(U)^{2}-(kG(U)-s_{2}(\tilde{C}_{3}+k\tilde{C}_{4}))G^{\prime}(U)+C_{2}{}^{2},

which is a second-order ODE for G⁡(U)G(U). Hence, the following result has been obtained.

Lemma 2.

The hodograph transformation

A=G′​(U)A=\sqrt{G^{\prime}(U)} (4.34)

converts the reduced ODE system (4.22)–(4.24) into a triangular form consisting of a second-order ODE (4.33) for G⁡(U)G(U), a first-order ODE (4.31) for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi), and an elementary ODE (4.28) for Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi).

Lemma 2 combined with Lemma 1 effectively provides a reduction of the original ODE system (4.22)–(4.24) to a single second-order ODE (4.33). As a consequence, phase-modulated travelling waves (1.3) can be obtained by the following direct method.

Theorem 1.

Any solution of the second-order ODE (4.33) for G⁡(U)G(U) yields a solution of the ODE system (4.22)–(4.24) by quadratures: First, integrate ODE (4.31), which is separable, to get U⁡(ξ)U(\xi). Second, substitute U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) into transformation (4.34) to get A⁡(ξ)A(\xi). Last, substitute A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) into ODE (4.24) and integrate to get Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi). The resulting expressions (U⁡(ξ),A⁡(ξ),Φ⁡(ξ))(U(\xi),A(\xi),\Phi(\xi)) give a phase-modulated travelling wave

u=U⁡(ξ),ψ=ei⁡(ω​t+Φ⁡(ξ))​A​(ξ),ξ=x−c​t.u=U(\xi),\quad\psi=e^{i(\omega t+\Phi(\xi))}A(\xi),\quad\xi=x-ct. (4.35)

Since non-trivial solutions of the ODE system (4.22)–(4.24) must have A≠const.A\neq\text{const.}, corresponding solutions of the second-order ODE (4.33) for G⁡(U)G(U) must satisfy

G′′​(U)≢0G^{\prime\prime}(U)\not\equiv 0 (4.36)

5. Abundant solitary wave solutions for nonlinearity powers p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4

The main result in Theorem 1 reduces the problem of obtaining explicit phase-modulated travelling waves (4.35) to the much more tractable problem of finding explicit solutions of the decoupled second-order ODE (4.33). Moreover, this ODE admits abundant polynomial solutions, which lead to explicit families of phase-modulated solitary waves, on zero and non-zero backgrounds, in the cases p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4. By comparison, starting with an ansatz for solutions of the original ODE system (4.4), as seen in Ref.[13, 14], yields only a few solutions in the case p=1p=1 and no solutions for p≥2p\geq 2.

In the next two subsections, the general polynomial form for solutions will be introduced and the types of phase-modulated solitary waves that arise from it will be characterized. In the final four subsections, the explicit solutions of the second-order ODE (4.33) will be summarized in each of the cases p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4, which leads to the phase-modulated solitary waves given in section 6.

5.1. Polynomial solutions of the decoupled ODE

The second-order ODE (4.33) for G⁡(U)G(U) is quadratic in GG, G′G^{\prime}, G′′G^{\prime\prime}, and also is polynomial in UU when pp is a positive integer. All polynomial solutions for G⁡(U)G(U) can be obtained by the following analysis.

First, the possible degree of a polynomial solution is determined by balancing powers in the ODE (4.33). Suppose that the highest power of UU in G⁡(U)G(U) is UqU^{q}, with q>1q>1 due to condition (4.36). Then, on the lefthand side in the ODE (4.33), the terms containing highest powers of UU are G⁡(U)​G′′​(U)2G(U)G^{\prime\prime}(U)^{2} and Up+2​G′′​(U)2U^{p+2}G^{\prime\prime}(U)^{2}, since p≥1p\geq 1. Their leading powers are, respectively, 3​q−43q-4 and 2​q+p−22q+p-2. On the righthand side, the terms containing highest powers of UU are U​G′​(U)2UG^{\prime}(U)^{2} and G⁡(U)​G′​(U)G(U)G^{\prime}(U), both of which have the leading power 2​q−12q-1. There are now several different possibilities for balancing powers.

The first possibility is to balance the leading powers on opposite sides. If 2​q+p−2>3​q−42q+p-2>3q-4, then this balance is given by 2​q+p−2=2​q−1>3​q−42q+p-2=2q-1>3q-4, which implies p=1p=1 and q<3q<3. If 2​q+p−2≤3​q−42q+p-2\leq 3q-4, then the balance is 3​q−4=2​q−1≥2​q+p−23q-4=2q-1\geq 2q+p-2 which implies q=3q=3 and p≤1p\leq 1. Thus, a consistent balance holds only for p=1p=1 and q≤3q\leq 3.

The second possibility is that the two terms with leading powers 2​q+p−22q+p-2 and 3​q−43q-4 cancel on the lefthand side, whereby the term with the subleading power must be balanced by the leading power term on the righthand side. In this case, equality of the powers 2​q+p−2=3​q−42q+p-2=3q-4 implies q=p+2q=p+2. Suppose the subleading term in G⁡(U)G(U) has power l<ql<q, l≥0l\geq 0. Then the subleading term on the lefthand side will be the leading term in (G⁡(U)+s1​s2​1(p+1)​(p+2)​Up+2)​G′′​(U)2(G(U)+s_{1}s_{2}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}U^{p+2})G^{\prime\prime}(U)^{2}, with corresponding highest power l+2​q−4=l+2​pl+2q-4=l+2p. The leading terms on the righthand side have highest power 2​q−1=2​p+32q-1=2p+3. Hence, the balance gives l=3l=3, with no restriction on pp.

The last possibility is that the two terms with leading power 2​q−12q-1 on the righthand side cancel each other, whereby the term with the subleading power must be balanced by the leading power term on the lefthand side. In this case, the cancellation requires that the highest power term in k​U​G′​(U)2−k​G​(U)​G′​(U)=k​G′​(U)​(U​G′​(U)−G⁡(U))kUG^{\prime}(U)^{2}-kG(U)G^{\prime}(U)=kG^{\prime}(U)(UG^{\prime}(U)-G(U)) vanishes. Clearly, this implies that q=1q=1, and thus no balance exists with q>1q>1.

The preceding possibilities can be merged into the form

G⁡(U)=−s1​s2​1(p+1)​(p+2)​Up+2+13​g3​U3+12​g2​U2+g1​U+g0,G(U)=-s_{1}s_{2}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}U^{p+2}+\tfrac{1}{3}g_{3}U^{3}+\tfrac{1}{2}g_{2}U^{2}+g_{1}U+g_{0}, (5.1)

where the coefficients g0,g1,g2,g3g_{0},g_{1},g_{2},g_{3} are constant parameters to be determined. When this polynomial form is substituted in the ODE (4.33), a polynomial equation of degree 2​p+32p+3 in UU is obtained. All solutions of interest will be listed after the discussion in the next subsection.

5.2. Classification of solitary wave solutions

Rather than systematically work out all solutions (U⁡(ξ),A⁡(ξ),Φ⁡(ξ))(U(\xi),A(\xi),\Phi(\xi)) produced by the polynomial form (5.1) for G⁡(U)G(U), it will be more effective to proceed by imposing conditions so that only solutions of physical interest will be obtained. This will considerably simplify the necessary steps to find (U⁡(ξ),A⁡(ξ),Φ⁡(ξ))(U(\xi),A(\xi),\Phi(\xi)).

As discussed in section 1, the solutions that will be of most physical interest describe phase-modulated solitary waves on either a zero background or a non-zero background. In particular, both A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) and U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) should have an exponentially localized profile that asymptotically approaches a constant as |ξ||\xi| goes to infinity.

The conditions under which such solutions will arise can be derived explicitly by studying the ODE (4.31) for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) appearing in Theorem 1. This ODE has the form of a nonlinear oscillator energy equation:

12U′+2V(U)=E,\tfrac{1}{2}U^{\prime}{}^{2}+V(U)=E, (5.2)

where, from the polynomial form (5.1) for G⁡(U)G(U),

V⁡(U)=s2​13​g3​U3+(s2​12​g2−12​c)​U2+(s2​g1−C1)​UV(U)=s_{2}\tfrac{1}{3}g_{3}U^{3}+(s_{2}\tfrac{1}{2}g_{2}-\tfrac{1}{2}c)U^{2}+(s_{2}g_{1}-C_{1})U (5.3)

represents the potential energy, and

E=C~4−s2​g0E=\tilde{C}_{4}-s_{2}g_{0} (5.4)

represents the total energy. Consequently, existence of solitary wave solutions for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) can be examined by using a standard energy analysis method applied to the potential (5.3).

To begin, observe that the potential is a cubic polynomial, which is independent of the nonlinearity power pp. The conditions for such a potential to support solitary waves on zero and non-zero backgrounds are well known from the cubic potential for travelling waves of the KdV equation: V⁡(U)V(U) must have both a local minimum and a local maximum. This requires that the discriminant of V′​(U)V^{\prime}(U) is positive,

d=(c−s2​g2)2+4​(s2​C1−g1)​g3>0.d=(c-s_{2}g_{2})^{2}+4(s_{2}C_{1}-g_{1})g_{3}>0. (5.5)

The resulting shape of the potential is shown in Fig. 1.

Proposition 5.

The potential (5.3) supports a single solitary wave, with EE being the local maximum of the potential. The corresponding solution for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) is given by

U⁡(ξ)=b+s3​h​sech2​(a​ξ),U(\xi)=b+s_{3}h\,{\rm sech}^{2}\big(\sqrt{a}\,\xi\big), (5.6)

where

h=32​d/|g3|,a=14​d,b=−s3​12​(d−c+s2​g2),E=(12​d+s3​13​|g3|)​b2,h=\tfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{d}/|g_{3}|,\quad a=\tfrac{1}{4}\sqrt{d},\quad b=-s_{3}\tfrac{1}{2}(\sqrt{d}-c+s_{2}g_{2}),\quad E=(\tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{d}+s_{3}\tfrac{1}{3}|g_{3}|)b^{2}, (5.7)

and

s3=s2​sgn​(g3)=±1.s_{3}=s_{2}\,{\rm sgn}(g_{3})=\pm 1. (5.8)

This solitary wave (5.6) will be bright (namely, a positive peak) when s3=+1s_{3}=+1, or dark (namely, a negative peak) when s3=−1s_{3}=-1. Its background is bb and its height/depth relative to the background is h>0h>0. Its width is proportional to w=2/aw=2/\sqrt{a}, with a>0a>0. The height/depth and width are related by h​w2=12/|g3|hw^{2}=12/|g_{3}|.

Fig. 2 illustrates bright and dark peaks for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi).

Next, from Theorem 1, the solutions for A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) and Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi) respectively are given by

A⁡(ξ)=g1+g2​U​(ξ)+g3​U​(ξ)2−s1​s2​1p+1​U​(ξ)p+1A(\xi)=\sqrt{g_{1}+g_{2}U(\xi)+g_{3}U(\xi)^{2}-s_{1}s_{2}\tfrac{1}{p+1}U(\xi)^{p+1}} (5.9)

and

Φ⁡(ξ)=c2​ξ±μ​∫0ξd​ξA​(ξ)2+ϕ,\Phi(\xi)=\frac{c}{2}\xi\pm\sqrt{\mu}\int_{0}^{\xi}\frac{d\xi}{A(\xi)^{2}}+\phi, (5.10)

where

ϕ and μ=C22\phi\quad\text{ and }\quad\mu=C_{2}{}^{2} (5.11)

are constants. When U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) has a localized profile, then so does A⁡(ξ)A(\xi), and thus the resulting solution will describe a solitary wave.

Some conditions are required for expressions (5.9)–(5.10) to be well-defined.

First, the square-root (5.9) must have

g1+g2​U​(ξ)+g3​U​(ξ)2−s1​s2​1p+1​U​(ξ)p+1≥0g_{1}+g_{2}U(\xi)+g_{3}U(\xi)^{2}-s_{1}s_{2}\tfrac{1}{p+1}U(\xi)^{p+1}\geq 0 (5.12)

for all ξ\xi. Since the extremal values of U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) are U⁡(±∞)=bU(\pm\infty)=b and U⁡(0)=b+s3​hU(0)=b+s_{3}h, necessary conditions are given by A​(±∞)2≥0A(\pm\infty)^{2}\geq 0 and A​(0)2≥0A(0)^{2}\geq 0, where

Second, if μ≠0\mu\neq 0, convergence of the integral (5.10) at ξ=0\xi=0 requires A​(0)2>0A(0)^{2}>0, since otherwise A⁡(0)=0A(0)=0 implies A​(ξ)2∼O⁡(ξ2)A(\xi)^{2}\sim O(\xi^{2}) as ξ∼0\xi\sim 0, which leads to a singularity at ξ=0\xi=0. Likewise, convergence for |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty requires A​(±∞)2>0A(\pm\infty)^{2}>0, since otherwise a singularity occurs due to A​(ξ)2∼O⁡(e−a​|ξ|)A(\xi)^{2}\sim O(e^{-a|\xi|}) as ξ∼±∞\xi\sim\pm\infty.

Therefore, the conditions

A​(±∞)2>0,A​(0)2>0, if ​μ≠0,\displaystyle A(\pm\infty)^{2}>0,\quad A(0)^{2}>0,\quad\text{ if }\mu\neq 0, (5.14a)
A​(±∞)2≥0,A​(0)2≥0, if ​μ=0,\displaystyle A(\pm\infty)^{2}\geq 0,\quad A(0)^{2}\geq 0,\quad\text{ if }\mu=0, (5.14b)

together with

h>0,a>0,μ≥0h>0,\quad a>0,\quad\mu\geq 0 (5.15)

are necessary. Note that if μ=0\mu=0 and A⁡(0)=A⁡(±∞)=0A(0)=A(\pm\infty)=0 then the full condition (5.12) must be checked.

Now, the final step will be to solve the second-order ODE (4.33) with G⁡(U)G(U) having the polynomial form (5.1). Hereafter, it will be convenient to re-parameterize this polynomial by using the solitary wave parameters b,h,a,Eb,h,a,E, and s3=±1s_{3}=\pm 1:

g0=s2​(C~4−E),g1=s2​(C1+2​b​h​a+s3​3​b2​a),g2=s2​(c−2​(h−s3​3​b)​a),g3=s2​s3​3​a.g_{0}=s_{2}(\tilde{C}_{4}-E),\quad g_{1}=s_{2}(C_{1}+2bha+s_{3}3b^{2}a),\quad g_{2}=s_{2}(c-2(h-s_{3}3b)a),\quad g_{3}=s_{2}s_{3}3a. (5.16)

It will also be useful to put

ω=ϖ−14​c2\omega=\varpi-\tfrac{1}{4}c^{2} (5.17)

in terms of a modified frequency parameter ϖ\varpi. Substitution of the re-parameterized polynomial expression (5.1) and (5.16)–(5.17) into the ODE (4.33) yields a polynomial equation in UU with powers 11, 22, 33, 44, 55, pp, p+1p+1, p+2p+2, p+3p+3, p+4p+4, 2​p2p, 2​p+12p+1, 2​p+22p+2, 2​p+32p+3, and with coefficients that involve the constants C1,C~3,EC_{1},\tilde{C}_{3},E (cf (5.4)), the solitary wave parameters b,h,ab,h,a, the physical constants p,k,ϖ,c,μp,k,\varpi,c,\mu, and the signs s1,s2,s3s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}, which are subject to the inequalities p≠0p\neq 0, k≠0k\neq 0, c≠0c\neq 0, h≠0h\neq 0, a≠0a\neq 0 as well as the sign conditions (2.10) and (5.8).

To solve the resulting polynomial equation, it must be split with respect to all distinct powers of UU. Since pp is an unknown, case distinctions arise when any two powers with at least one involving pp are equal. In each such case, the splitting gives an overdetermined algebraic system for the unknowns C1,C~3,E,p,k,b,h,a,c,ϖ,μC_{1},\tilde{C}_{3},E,p,k,b,h,a,c,\varpi,\mu, and s1,s2,s3s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}. All of the case distinctions and subsequent splitting and solving of the algebraic system have been carried out by using the computer algebra package Crack [24]. Further computational remarks are summarized in Appendix A.

This computational analysis shows that solutions exist only for p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4. For each case, explicit expressions for g1g_{1}, g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}, EE, and the determined parameters among b,h,a,μ,ϖ,c,kb,h,a,\mu,\varpi,c,k and also the signs s1,s2,s3s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}, are given in Appendix B.

Simplification of the solutions followed by analysis of the conditions (5.14) and (5.15) has been done in Maple. This step is highly non-trivial and relies heavily on the use of the parameterization in terms of b,h,a,c,ϖ,μb,h,a,c,\varpi,\mu. A key aspect is finding an optimal subset of these parameters for each solution such that, firstly, there are no unsolved algebraic equations, and secondly, conditions (5.14) and (5.15) reduce to a simple form characterized by a minimal set of inequalities holding on the free parameters. In some cases, a case splitting arises from this reduction, through the two subcases μ≠0\mu\neq 0 and μ=0\mu=0 in the conditions (5.14), since the solution of the inequalities can have disconnected components when μ=0\mu=0. The best outcome turns out to be achieved by giving a lower priority for bb to be solved for among the set of parameters rather than assuming that cc should be an arbitrary free parameter. This analysis is shown in Appendix B.

A classification of the resulting set of solution families is summarized in Table 1. These solution families will be listed in the subsequent four subsections. Every family determines a corresponding explicit gKdV-LS solution (5.6)–(5.10) for (U⁡(ξ),A⁡(ξ),Φ⁡(ξ))(U(\xi),A(\xi),\Phi(\xi)), which are presented and discussed in section 6.

A final remark here is that the lack of solutions for any p>4p>4 is likely due to the limitation of considering only a polynomial form (5.1) for G⁡(U)G(U). It should be possible to extend the computational analysis to a rational form for G⁡(U)G(U), which may yield additional solutions, possibly involving higher powers for pp. Such a form could also be relevant for seeking non-solitary wave solutions of the ODE system (4.4), such as heavy-tail solutions which have a power decay for large |ξ||\xi| [28].

6. Phase-modulated solitary waves

From the results in section 5, the explicit solitary wave solutions (4.35) of the gKdV-LS system (2.8)–(2.9) will now be presented and their kinematic features will be discussed. These solutions hold for the nonlinearity powers p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4, covering all physically interesting cases for the nonlinearity in the gKdV-LS system.

The gKdV variable u=U⁡(ξ)u=U(\xi) is given by the sech-squared expression (5.6). Physically, it describes a solitary wave on a background bb, with a height/depth h>0h>0, where the wave is bright when s3>0s_{3}>0 and dark when s3<0s_{3}<0. Its width is proportional to w=2/aw=2/\sqrt{a} in terms of the parameter a>0a>0.

The LS variable ψ=A⁡(ξ)​exp⁡(i⁡(ω​t+Φ⁡(ξ))CLOSE\psi=A(\xi)\exp(i(\omega t+\Phi(\xi)) is given by the amplitude expression (5.9) and the phase expression (5.10). These expressions exhibit a wide variety of features.

The amplitude A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) has the form of a solitary wave which is the square-root of a linear combination of U⁡(ξ)U(\xi), U​(ξ)2U(\xi)^{2}, U​(ξ)p+1U(\xi)^{p+1} terms plus a constant term. Note that the resulting profile for A⁡(ξ)A(\xi) can contain up to 2​p+12p+1 local peaks on a tail (background) A∞=A⁡(±∞)A_{\infty}=A(\pm\infty), with the central peak at ξ=0\xi=0 having the amplitude A0=A⁡(0)A_{0}=A(0), as given by expressions (5.13). This central peak will be bright/dark if A′′​(0)≷0A^{\prime\prime}(0)\gtrless 0 respectively, while the tail will be called bright/dark if A∞≷A0A_{\infty}\gtrless A_{0}. These features are illustrated in Fig. 3.

Side peaks occur in symmetrical pairs. Their location and height can be found straightforwardly by considering

B⁡(z)=A​(1a​arccosh​(1/z))2=g1+g2​(b+s3​h​z)+g3​(b+s3​h​z)2−s1​s2​1p+1​(b+s3​h​z)p+1,B(z)=A\big(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}}{\rm arccosh}(1/\sqrt{z})\big)^{2}=g_{1}+g_{2}(b+s_{3}hz)+g_{3}(b+s_{3}hz)^{2}-s_{1}s_{2}\tfrac{1}{p+1}(b+s_{3}hz)^{p+1}, (6.1)

which is polynomial of degree p+1p+1 in z=sech​(a​ξ)2z={\rm sech}(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)^{2} with 0<z≤10<z\leq 1. In this interval, each non-zero root z=z∗z=z^{*} of

B′​(z)=s3​h​(g2+2​g3​(b+s3​h​z)−s1​s2​(b+s3​h​z)p)=0B^{\prime}(z)=s_{3}h(g_{2}+2g_{3}(b+s_{3}hz)-s_{1}s_{2}(b+s_{3}hz)^{p})=0 (6.2)

determines that a pair of side peaks exist at OPENξ∗=±1a​arccosh​(1/z∗))2\xi^{*}=\pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}}{\rm arccosh}(1/\sqrt{z^{*}})\big)^{2}. These peaks will be bright/dark if H′′​(z∗)≷0H^{\prime\prime}(z^{*})\gtrless 0 respectively. The case of one pair of side peaks is illustrated in Fig. 3 .

The phase Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi) is given by a linear term in ξ\xi plus a quadrature term that is odd in ξ\xi with a coefficient ±μ\pm\sqrt{\mu}. In the case when this coefficient vanishes, the phase is thereby linear in ξ\xi

Φ⁡(ξ)=c2​ξ+ϕ, if ​μ=0.\Phi(\xi)=\frac{c}{2}\xi+\phi,\quad\text{ if }\mu=0. (6.3)

In the general case, μ>0\mu>0, the quadrature term in the phase can be expressed more conveniently as the integral of a rational function, based on the identities sech2​(arctanh⁡(ζ))=1−ζ2{\rm sech}^{2}({\rm arctanh}(\zeta))=1-\zeta^{2} and arctanh′​(ζ)=1/(1−ζ2){\rm arctanh}^{\prime}(\zeta)=1/(1-\zeta^{2}):

∫0ξd​ξA​(ξ)2=1a​∫0tanh⁡(a​ξ)d​ζ(1−ζ2)​B​(1−ζ2),\int_{0}^{\xi}\frac{d\xi}{A(\xi)^{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}\int_{0}^{\tanh(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)}\frac{d\zeta}{(1-\zeta^{2})B(1-\zeta^{2})}, (6.4)

where the degree of B⁡(1−ζ2)B(1-\zeta^{2}) as a polynomial in ζ2\zeta^{2} is p+1p+1. For ξ→±∞\xi\to\pm\infty, this quadrature has the asymptotic behaviour

∫0ξd​ξA​(ξ)2∼1A∞2​ξ+sgn⁡(ξ)​∫0∞(1A​(ξ)2−1A∞2)​𝑑ξ,\int_{0}^{\xi}\frac{d\xi}{A(\xi)^{2}}\sim\frac{1}{A_{\infty}^{2}}\,\xi+{\rm sgn}(\xi)\int_{0}^{\infty}\Big(\frac{1}{A(\xi)^{2}}-\frac{1}{A_{\infty}^{2}}\Big)d\xi, (6.5)

where A∞≠0A_{\infty}\neq 0 due to condition (5.14). This motivates a decomposition of Φ⁡(ξ)\Phi(\xi) into linear and nonlinear terms:

Φ⁡(ξ)=Φlin.​(ξ)+Φnonlin.​(ξ)+ϕ if ​μ>0,\Phi(\xi)=\Phi_{\text{lin.}}(\xi)+\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\xi)+\phi\quad\text{ if }\mu>0, (6.6)

Φnonlin.​(ξ)=\displaystyle\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\xi)= ±μa​∫0tanh⁡(a​ξ)(1B⁡(1−ζ2)−1A∞2)​d​ζ(1−ζ2).\displaystyle\frac{\pm\sqrt{\mu}}{\sqrt{a}}\int_{0}^{\tanh(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)}\Big(\frac{1}{B(1-\zeta^{2})}-\frac{1}{A_{\infty}^{2}}\Big)\frac{d\zeta}{(1-\zeta^{2})}.

Evaluation of Φnonlin.​(ξ)\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\xi) will yield a linear combination of arctan and arctanh (or ln) functions in terms of ζ=tanh⁡(a​ξ)\zeta=\tanh(\sqrt{a}\,\xi). Note that its graph will be kink shaped, since Φnonlin.​(∞)=−Φnonlin.​(−∞)\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\infty)=-\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(-\infty) and Φnonlin.​(0)=0\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(0)=0. The sign of the kink is determined by the slope of Φnonlin.​(ξ)\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\xi) at ξ=0\xi=0:

sgn⁡(Φnonlin.​(∞))=sgn⁡(Φnonlin.′​(0))=±sgn⁡(A∞−A0){\rm sgn}(\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\infty))={\rm sgn}(\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}^{\prime}(0))=\pm{\rm sgn}(A_{\infty}-A_{0}) (6.8)

using condition (5.14), where “±\pm” refers to the sign in expressions (6.7). Consequently, the asymptotic behaviour of the phase is

Φ⁡(ξ)∼ϕ+Φlin.​(ξ)±Φnonlin.​(∞)​ as ​ξ→±∞\Phi(\xi)\sim\phi+\Phi_{\text{lin.}}(\xi)\pm\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\infty)\text{ as }\xi\to\pm\infty (6.9)

in terms of the asymptote Φnonlin.​(∞)≠0\Phi_{\text{nonlin.}}(\infty)\neq 0 of the kink.

All of these features, in addition to the sign of the wave speed cc and the gKdV-LS coupling kk, are summarized for each nonlinearity power p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4 in the next section (cf Tables 2 to  8).

6.1. Features of solitary wave solutions

6.2. Conserved integrals

All of the solitary wave solutions (4.35) with expressions (5.6), (5.9), (5.10) have a total mass, charge, momentum, and energy given respectively by the four conserved integrals (4.5)–(4.8). The latter two integrals (4.7)–(4.8) can be simplified by use of the ODEs (4.23) for U⁡(ξ)U(\xi) and (4.24) for Φ⁡(z)\Phi(z).

Each integral will be finite if uu has a zero background and |ψ||\psi| has a zero tail, namely b=0b=0 and g1=0g_{1}=0, since then the density goes to 00 exponentially in |ξ||\xi|.

If a density otherwise has a non-zero asymptotic tail as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty, the conserved integral will diverge. Nevertheless, the divergent contribution can be removed by subtraction of the asymptotic tail in the density, yielding a regularized integral which is conserved and finite.

The regularized integrals for mass, charge, momentum, and energy are given by

M~​[U]=∫−∞∞(U−b)​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle\tilde{M}[U]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(U-b)\,d\xi, (6.10)
J~​[A]=∫−∞∞12​(A2−A02)​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle\tilde{J}[A]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\tfrac{1}{2}(A^{2}-A_{0}^{2})\,d\xi, (6.11)
P~​[U,A,Φ]=∫−∞∞(12​(U2−b2)−s2​c2​k​(A2−A02))​𝑑ξ,\displaystyle\tilde{P}[U,A,\Phi]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}(U^{2}-b^{2})-s_{2}\tfrac{c}{2k}(A^{2}-A_{0}^{2})\big)\,d\xi, (6.12)
H~​[U,A,Φ]=∫−∞∞(12U′2+s21kA′2−s11(p+1)​(p+2)(Up+2−bp+2)OPEN+s2​c24​k​(A2−A02)−s2​(U​A2−b​A02))​d​ξ=∫−∞∞(12​(U2−b2)+C1​(U−b)−s1​2(p+1)​(p+2)​(Up+2−bp+2)CLOSEOPEN−s2​ωk​(A2−A02)−s2​2​(U​A2−b​A02))​d​ξ,\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \tilde{H}[U,A,\Phi]=&\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}U^{\prime}{}^{2}+s_{2}\tfrac{1}{k}A^{\prime}{}^{2}-s_{1}\tfrac{1}{(p+1)(p+2)}(U^{p+2}-b^{p+2})\\ &\qquad+s_{2}\tfrac{c^{2}}{4k}(A^{2}-A_{0}^{2})-s_{2}(UA^{2}-bA_{0}^{2})\big)\,d\xi\\ =&\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\big(\tfrac{1}{2}(U^{2}-b^{2})+C_{1}(U-b)-s_{1}\tfrac{2}{(p+1)(p+2)}(U^{p+2}-b^{p+2})\\ &\qquad-s_{2}\tfrac{\omega}{k}(A^{2}-A_{0}^{2})-s_{2}2(UA^{2}-bA_{0}^{2})\big)\,d\xi,\end{aligned} (6.13)

which are finite for all solitary wave solutions (5.6), (5.9), (5.10).

It is straightforward to evaluate the mass integral (6.10):

M~​[U]=∫−∞∞s3​h​sech2​(a​ξ)​𝑑ξ=s3​2​ha.\tilde{M}[U]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}s_{3}h\,{\rm sech}^{2}(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)d\xi=s_{3}\frac{2h}{\sqrt{a}}. (6.14)

This is the same general expression as the mass of the mKdV solitary wave and depends on pp only implicitly through hh when it is evaluated for a specific solution family.

It is similarly straightforward to evaluate the charge integral (6.11) for each power p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4, where the density is given by 12​g3​h2​sech4​(a​ξ)+s3​12​(2​b​g3+g2)​h​sech2​(a​ξ)+s1​s2​12​(p+1)​(bp+1−(s3​h​sech2​(a​ξ)+b)p+1)\frac{1}{2}g_{3}h^{2}\,{\rm sech}^{4}(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)+s_{3}\frac{1}{2}(2bg_{3}+g_{2})h\,{\rm sech}^{2}(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)+s_{1}s_{2}\frac{1}{2(p+1)}\big(b^{p+1}-\big(s_{3}h\,{\rm sech}^{2}(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)+b\big)^{p+1}\big). Alternatively, a single expression that holds for all pp can be obtained by applying the following integration steps to the third term in the density. Make a binomial expansion of this term and change the integration variable via sech⁡(a​ξ)=2​y/(1+y2){\rm sech}(\sqrt{a}\,\xi)=2y/(1+y^{2}). Since the density is even in ξ\xi, the charge integral can be expressed as twice the expanded density integrated over yy from 00 to 11. Each term is given by an associated Legendre function and the sum of all the terms can be shown to yield a generalized hypergeometric function F23{}_{3}F_{2} [29]. When combined with the integral of the first and second terms in the density, this gives a simple general expression

J~[U]=s3ha(2g3(b+s3h/3)+g2+s1s2bpF23([1,1,−p],[3/2,2],−s3h/b)),p=1,2,3,4.\tilde{J}[U]=s_{3}\frac{h}{\sqrt{a}}\Big(2g_{3}(b+s_{3}h/3)+g_{2}+s_{1}s_{2}b^{p}\,{}_{3}F_{2}\big([1,1,-p],[3/2,2],{-s_{3}}h/b\big)\Big),\quad p=1,2,3,4. (6.15)

This expression involves pp explicitly as well as implicitly through b,h,g2,g3b,h,g_{2},g_{3} when it is evaluated for a specific solution family. The generalized hypergeometric function F23([1,1,−p],[3/2,2],−s3h/b){}_{3}F_{2}\big([1,1,-p],[3/2,2],{-s_{3}}h/b\big) is a polynomial of degree pp in h/bh/b.

The same steps can be used to evaluate the momentum and energy integrals, which yields the respective expressions

P~​[U,A,Φ]=s3​hk​a​(CLOSE2​(k−s2​c​g3)​(b+s3​h/3)−s2​c​g2+s1cbp3F2([1,1,−p],[3/2,2],−s3h/b)),p=1,2,3,4;\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \tilde{P}[U,A,\Phi]=s_{3}\frac{h}{k\sqrt{a}}\Big(&2(k-s_{2}cg_{3})(b+s_{3}h/3)-s_{2}cg_{2}\\ &\quad+s_{1}cb^{p}\,{}_{3}F_{2}\big([1,1,-p],[3/2,2],{-s_{3}}h/b\big)\Big),\quad p=1,2,3,4;\end{aligned} (6.16)
E~​[U,A,Φ]=s3​ha​(CLOSEs2​4​(g3​(b+s3​h/3)2−(g3​(b+s3​h/3)+g2/2)​(4​(b+s3​h/3)+ω/k)CLOSE−g3h2/5−g1)+2c(b+s3h/3)+2C1+s12bp(2b3F2([1,1,−p−1],[3/2,2],−s3h/b)+ω/k3F2([1,1,−p],[3/2,2],−s3h/b))),p=1,2,3,4.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \tilde{E}[U,A,\Phi]=s_{3}\frac{h}{\sqrt{a}}\Big(&s_{2}4\big(g_{3}(b+s_{3}h/3)^{2}-(g_{3}(b+s_{3}h/3)+g_{2}/2)(4(b+s_{3}h/3)+\omega/k)\\ &\qquad-g_{3}h^{2}/5-g_{1}\big)+2c(b+s_{3}h/3)+2C_{1}\\ &\quad+s_{1}2b^{p}\big(2b\,{}_{3}F_{2}\big([1,1,-p-1],[3/2,2],{-s_{3}}h/b\big)\\ &\qquad\qquad\quad+\omega/k\,{}_{3}F_{2}\big([1,1,-p],[3/2,2],{-s_{3}}h/b\big)\big)\Big),\quad p=1,2,3,4.\end{aligned} (6.17)
Proposition 6.

Solitary wave solutions (5.6), (5.9), (5.10) have regularized mass (6.14), charge (6.15), momentum (6.16), and energy (6.17), all of which are finite.

6.3. Remarks on stability

A basic notion of stability for a solution (U⁡(ξ),A⁡(ξ),Φ⁡(z))(U(\xi),A(\xi),\Phi(z)) is linear (spectral) stability under perturbations. For a parametric family of solutions, a stronger notion is orbital stability. Both notions are related to convexity of the integral quantity (4.9) in the variational principle (4.10) for the ODE system (4.4) that determines solutions. In the case of solutions that have a non-zero background, a regularized version of this integral quantity can be used,

W~​[U,A,Φ]=H~​[U,A,Φ]+c​P~​[U,A,Φ]−s2​(2​ω/k)​J~​[A]+C1​M~​[U],\widetilde{W}[U,A,\Phi]=\tilde{H}[U,A,\Phi]+c\tilde{P}[U,A,\Phi]-s_{2}(2\omega/k)\tilde{J}[A]+C_{1}\tilde{M}[U], (6.18)

where the conserved integrals (4.5)–(4.8) are replaced by their regularized counterparts (6.10)–(6.13), which does not change the Euler-Lagrange ODEs.

Convexity is determined by the eigenvalues of the Hessian operator of the regularized integral quantity (6.18). After reverting from amplitude and phase variables to the LS variable (4.3), the Hessian is given by matrix operator

∂2W~​[U,Ψ,Ψ¯;p]=\displaystyle\partial^{2}\widetilde{W}[U,\Psi,\bar{\Psi};p]= (6.19)
−(d2d​ξ2−c+s1​Ups2​Ψ¯s2​Ψs2​Ψ(s2/k)​(d2d​ξ2−i​c​dd​ξ+ω)+s2​U0s2​Ψ¯0(s2/k)​(d2d​ξ2+i​c​dd​ξ+ω)+s2​U).\displaystyle-\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{d^{2}}{d\xi^{2}}-c+s_{1}U^{p}&s_{2}\bar{\Psi}&s_{2}\Psi\\ s_{2}\Psi&(s_{2}/k)\Big(\dfrac{d^{2}}{d\xi^{2}}-ic\dfrac{d}{d\xi}+\omega\Big)+s_{2}U&0\\ s_{2}\bar{\Psi}&0&(s_{2}/k)\Big(\dfrac{d^{2}}{d\xi^{2}}+ic\dfrac{d}{d\xi}+\omega\Big)+s_{2}U\end{pmatrix}.

This operator is formally self-adjoint with respect to a joint L2L^{2} inner product for the UU-component and a hermitian L2L^{2} inner product for the Ψ,Ψ¯\Psi,\bar{\Psi}-components. It can be brought to a diagonal form by the change of variables

Ψ=s2​(k/2)​ei​c2​ξ​(Θ1+i​Θ2),Θ¯1=Θ1,Θ¯2=Θ2,\Psi=s_{2}(k/2)e^{i\frac{c}{2}\xi}(\Theta_{1}+i\Theta_{2}),\quad\bar{\Theta}_{1}=\Theta_{1},\quad\bar{\Theta}_{2}=\Theta_{2}, (6.20)

yielding

ℒ=ℐ​d2d​ξ2+𝒱{\mathcal{L}}={\mathcal{I}}\dfrac{d^{2}}{d\xi^{2}}+{\mathcal{V}} (6.21)

with

ℐ=diag⁡(1,s2​k/2,s2​k/2),𝒱=(−c+s1​Ups2​(k2/2)​Θ1s2​(k2/2)​Θ2s2​(k2/2)​Θ1s2​(k/2)​(ϖ+k​U)0s2​(k2/2)​Θ20s2​(k/2)​(ϖ+k​U)),{\mathcal{I}}={\rm diag}\big(1,s_{2}k/2,s_{2}k/2\big),\quad{\mathcal{V}}=\begin{pmatrix}-c+s_{1}U^{p}&s_{2}(k^{2}/2)\Theta_{1}&s_{2}(k^{2}/2)\Theta_{2}\\ s_{2}(k^{2}/2)\Theta_{1}&s_{2}(k/2)(\varpi+kU)&0\\ s_{2}(k^{2}/2)\Theta_{2}&0&s_{2}(k/2)(\varpi+kU)\end{pmatrix}, (6.22)

where ϖ\varpi is expression (5.17). This is a linear self-adjoint matrix operator with respect to a real L2L^{2} inner product for the real components (U,Θ1,Θ2)(U,\Theta_{1},\Theta_{2}).

From Proposition 4, there are three infinitesimal symmetries (4.11)–(4.12) of the Euler-Lagrange ODEs (4.4). A standard argument shows that the translation and phase rotation symmetries will each give rise to a zero eigenvalue of the operator (6.21). The key question for determining stability is whether this operator has a negative eigenvalue [30]. This will be addressed in subsequent work.

7. Concluding remarks

The new method developed in the present work has yielded 22 families of exact solitary wave solutions (1.3) for the coupled nonlinear gKdV-LS system (1.1)–(1.2) with nonlinearity powers p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4. No solutions for p>1p>1 were known previously.

For p=1p=1, four of the solution families contain the solitary waves that were first found in Ref.[7, 13]. The former one arose in the context of nonlinear plasma waves and coincides with the first of the two families 1-i.1 (i.e. dark LS peak). The latter ones come from nonlinear waves in anharmonic lattices and were named bright/dark Davydov solitons of the 1st and 2nd kind: they are respectively given by the case s2=−1s_{2}=-1 of families 1-ii with μ≠0\mu\neq 0 and 1-ii.1; and the case k=1/6k=1/6 of family 1-i with μ=0\mu=0 and c<ccrit.c<c_{\text{crit.}} and the case k=1/6k=1/6 of the second family 1-i.1 (i.e. bright LS peak). These particular solitary waves are characterized by respective relations |ψ|2∝|\psi|^{2}\propto (u−b)​(u−u0)(u-b)(u-u_{0}), u−bu-b, (u−u0)2(u-u_{0})^{2}, for some constant u0u_{0}, which allows them to be derived by basic ODE methods. The corresponding relations for the travelling wave ODE system (1.4) have the form A2∝A^{2}\propto (U−b)​(U−U0)(U-b)(U-U_{0}), U−bU-b, (U−U0)2(U-U_{0})^{2} in terms of the variables (4.3).

The additional five solution families for p=1p=1 describe new solitary waves. Physical properties and applications, as well as stability analysis based on the variational principle (4.10), for all of the new solution families for p=1,2,3,4p=1,2,3,4 will be discussed elsewhere.

The main results obtained here illustrate the power of modern symmetry analysis methods combined with advanced symbolic computation packages for the study of exact solitary wave solutions of coupled nonlinear ODE systems.

As further applications, one direction would be a generalization of the gKdV-LS system to include a self-interaction ν​|ψ|q​ψ\nu|\psi|^{q}\psi in equation (1.2) for the Schrodinger field ψ\psi, where q>0q>0 is a nonlinearity power. Only a few exact solutions are known for this nonlinear coupled system [31]. Another direction would be to consider a coupled Boussinesq-LS system [32] and its pp-power generalizations, for which exact solitary wave solutions are of physical interest.

A more general direction would be to extend the present method to the study of nonlinearly generalized Hénon-Heiles ODE systems, which arise in wide variety of physical and applied mathematical problems.

Appendix A Computational remarks

The computation leading to the results summarized in Table 1 will be outlined here.

As explained in Section 5.2, the computation involves solving a polynomial equation obtained by substitution of the general polynomial ansatz (5.1) into the ODE (4.33) for G⁡(U)G(U). This polynomial equation has 436 terms, containing 16 powers 0,1,2,3,4,5,p,p+1,p+2,p+3,p+4,2​p,2​p+1,2​p+2,2​p+30,1,2,3,4,5,p,p+1,p+2,p+3,p+4,2p,2p+1,2p+2,2p+3. There are 14 unknowns, consisting of pp, kk, bb, hh, aa, cc, ϖ\varpi, μ\mu, C1C_{1}, C~3\tilde{C}_{3}, EE, and s1,s2,s3s_{1},s_{2},s_{3}, which are required to obey 8 conditions, p≠0,−1p\neq 0,-1, k≠0k\neq 0, h≠0h\neq 0, a≠0a\neq 0, c≠0c\neq 0, and s12=s22=s32=1s_{1}{}^{2}=s_{2}{}^{2}=s_{3}{}^{2}=1. These conditions together with the polynomial equation constitute the algebraic system to be solved. This is a non-polynomial algebraic problem, because pp appears in exponents and because products of the unknowns (including pp) appear in the coefficients of some terms.

The computer algebra package Crack [24], written in REDUCE, is able to solve nonlinear problems (algebraic as well as differential). Specifically, it is able to split equations with respect to independent variables, including when a variable appears as an exponent. It is also able to make case distinctions as needed. In an automatic run, all splitting with respect to the independent variables has a high priority.

The system here has a single independent variable, UU. Crack splits the system with respect to UU if all exponents are known to be different. Since pp is an unknown that appears in exponents, Crack proceeds by systematically taking the difference between two exponents, with at least one of the exponents containing pp, and starting a case distinction in which the pivot is given by the expression for the difference being zero or non-zero. In the non-zero case, this inequality is simply appended to the system. In the zero case, Crack determines pp and then substitutes it back into the system. If the resulting system either has all exponents of UU being distinct, or has no exponents of UU involving pp, then it can be split into a system of algebraic equations that involve only the unknowns. Crack is able to solve these equations straightforwardly. If an equation factorizes, then a further case distinction is made with respect to each factor. This process is repeated until all possible case distinctions have been considered, and the system has been either fully solved or reduced to irreducible equations such as high degree polynomials in the unknowns. In the system under consideration, every case leads to an algebraic system that is explicitly solved in the sense that its solution is given by explicit expressions together with at most low-degree polynomials whose solution set is non-empty.

The final result is 56 solutions that can be merged into non-overlapping families organized by pp as shown in Table 9.
